html:
The capture and sale of Europeans and others by corsairs from the ports of North Africa, from the early 1500s to the early 1800s. The main bases were Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli and Salé in Morocco.

Corsairs, privateers with licences from their rulers, seized merchant ships and raided coastal villages, above all in Italy, Spain and Portugal, but as far away as Ireland and Iceland. Captives were sold in the markets of Algiers and other ports. Men rowed the galleys or worked in quarries and building; women served in households. Some were ransomed; some converted to Islam. The Spanish writer Miguel de Cervantes spent five years as a captive in Algiers. Estimates of the total run to hundreds of thousands, perhaps more than a million, but are disputed.

The trade was one side of a long sea war: Christian corsairs, such as the Knights of Malta, enslaved Muslims in the same way. The North African states were nominally part of the Ottoman Empire. The raids ended after the Barbary Wars with the United States, a British and Dutch bombardment of Algiers in 1816, and the French conquest of Algiers in 1830.
